la:noun:Pygmalion.html:
Pygmălĭon, ōnis, m., = Πυγμαλίων.
Grandson of Agenor, who became enamoured of a statue he had made, and to which, at his earnest petition, Venus gave life, ; .—
Son of Belus, king of Tyre, and brother of Dido, ; ; .—Hence,
Pygmălĭōnēus, a, um, adj., Pygmalionian, poet. for Phœnician: terra,; also for Carthaginian, .

la:noun:pyra.html:
pўra, ae, f., = πυρά.
A funeral pile, pyre (pure Lat. rogus), ; ; ; ; Auct. B. Afr. 91; .—
A fire, .—
Pўra, ae, f., the name of the place on Mount Œta where Hercules is said to have burned himself, .

la:other:Pyrgi.gloss: a city on the coast of Etruria, near Alsium and port of Caere
senses: a city on the coast of Etruria, near Alsium and port of Caere
la:other:Pyrgi.html:
Pyrgi, ōrum, m., = Πύργοι,
a colony in Etruria, now the village of S. Severa, ; ; Liv 36, 3, 6; ; ; ; cf. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 296 sq. — Hence,
Pyrgensis, e, adj., of or belonging to Pyrgi, Pyrgan: scorta, Lucil. ap. : Antistius,of Pyrgi,: publicanus,.

la:other:Pythagoras.html:
Pȳthăgŏras, ae, m., = Πυθαγόρας,
a celebrated philosopher of Samos, about 550 B.C.; he taught in Lower Italy (Croton and Metapontum), and was the founder of the Pythagorean philosophy, which received its name from him, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .— The Greek letter γ (called littera Pythagorae), with its two divergent arms, was used by Pythagoras as a symbol of the two diverse paths of life, that of virtue and of vice, ; cf. ; v. also .—Hence,
Pȳthăgŏrēus or Pȳthăgŏrīus, a, um, adj., = Πυθαγόρειος,Pythagorean: somnia,: dogma, Lab. ap. : pavo,into which, according to the Pythagorean doctrine of metempsychosis, the soul of Euphorbus had passed before it reached Pythagoras,: brassica,highly recommended by Pythagoras,in lemm. (cf. ): mos,.—Plur, subst.: Pȳthă-gŏrēi (-ŏrīi), ōrum, m., the followers of the Pythagorean philosophy, the Pythagoreans, ; —
Pȳthăgŏrĭcus, a, um, adj., = ΠυθαγορικόςPythagorean: libri,: philosophia, (an interpolated passage, v. Sillig in loc.): prudentia, (but Pythagorii, B. and K.; cf. Madv. Opusc. Ac. 1, p. 512).

la:adj:pygmaeus.gloss: Of or pertaining to a pygmy or dwarf, especially to the mythical Pygmaeī of Africa.
senses: Of or pertaining to a pygmy or dwarf, especially to the mythical Pygmaeī of Africa.

la:noun:pyrites.html:
pўrītes, ae, m., = πυρίτης.
Flint, . —
A millstone, .—
Iron pyrites, sulphuret of iron, marcasite, .

la:noun:Pyramus.html:
Pȳrămus, i, m., = Πύραμος,
the lover of Thisbe, who, on account of her supposed death, stabbed himself under a mulberry-tree, — Hence,
Pȳrămĕus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pyramus, Pyramian: arbor,i. e. the mulberry-tree,.

la:other:Pylades.gloss: Pylades (a Phocian prince known for his relationship with his cousin Orestes, son of Agamemnon)
senses: Pylades (a Phocian prince known for his relationship with his cousin Orestes, son of Agamemnon)
la:other:Pylades.html:
Pўlădes, ae and is, m., = Πυλάδης.
Son of King Strophius, celebrated as the friend of Orestes, ; ; ; ; ; ; and 120.— Transf., for a faithful friend, .—Dat. Pyladi, .—Hence,
Pўlădēus, a, um, adj., Pyladean; transf., for very faithful, very tender: amicitia,.—
A celebrated paniomimist from Cilicia, under Augustus, ; Sen. Excerpt. cont. 3 praef.; .

senses: A priestess of Pythian Apollo; Pythia
la:noun:pythia.html: Pȳthĭa, ae and ōrum, v. Pythius, sub Python, II. B. 1. and 2.

la:noun:pyramis.html:
pȳrămis, ĭdis, f., = πυραμις (prob. Egyptian),
a pyramid, ; ; ; ; : pyramidas regum miramur,; ; ; .—
Transf., a geometrical solid figure, a pyramid, Boëth. Arith. 2, 21 sqq.

la:noun:pyxis.gloss: a small box; for holding medicines or toiletries
senses: a small box; for holding medicines or toiletries
la:noun:pyxis.html:
pyxis (puxis, ; ), ĭdis, f., = πυξίς.
Lit., a box, a small box, esp. for unguents, medicines, etc. — Orig., of boxes made of boxwood, then of those of any kind of wood, and finally, also, of metallic boxes: veneni,: aurea,; cf. : cornea,: plumbea,.—Belonging to the toilet of women, ; (al. buxides).—
Transf.: ferrea,an iron cap fitted to the lower end of a pestle,.
